profiles.subject: Theotokos

overview.text: Gerontissa is Pantokrator Monastery’s principal revered Marian image. The monastery explains its name through the tradition of a dying elder who wished to receive Communion.
overview.reason: Necessary concise source-bound explanation;substantial modern text is not established as freely reproducible. This is an AI-written summary,not the source author’s wording.

blocks.text: The displayed Gerontissa shows the Mother of God standing alone, without Christ in her arms. Her body and hands turn to one side. A metal revetment covers much of the figure; the face and the long vertical form remain visible. This is a specific full-length composition, not a seated Mother-and-Child panel.

blocks.text: The monastery places the icon’s history near its fourteenth-century foundation but distinguishes that history from the painted appearance, which it dates to the nineteenth century. It relates a period in a well during pirate raids. Its location moved from behind the altar into the main church after the event associated with the elder.

blocks.text: In the received account, the celebrant delays while the elder is near death; the Mother of God’s voice from the icon urges him to act. The elder receives Communion and reposes. The monastery explicitly treats this as Athonite tradition.

blocks.text: An 1869 coloured engraving by Ioannis Kaldis records the standing composition with miniature scenes of the monastery, the finding in the well and the filling of empty oil jars. That dated print provides a separate historical witness to the nineteenth-century imagery.
